name.v: Intake: where a turn comes from

description.v: The peak of the cycle: everything addressed to the chat lands here — a human reply, a receipt for a finished background call, a sub-agent's report — and only from here is a turn born.

doc.v:
# Input and output
Input: a client message over the protocol, a background call's result, a sub-agent's report. Output: a started or resumed turn.

# Description
A turn is born not from the human pressing "send," but from something sitting in the chat's inbox. The difference shows up when a reply is written into a busy chat: it lands in the inbox and gets picked up by the turn already running.

The path of a message: client (web, command line, desktop shell) → protocol → router → chat inbox. The boundary between client and core runs through the router: whatever one client can do, any client can do, because it does it through the protocol. The chat's render stays one: the desktop shell shows the same web client in an embedded browser, not its own copy.

Two things then take over:

- the turn dispatcher, one per chat: takes from the inbox and starts a run. While a run is going, the next reply waits right there, so parallel turns in one chat never happen by construction, and Stop kills everything at once — the current turn and the queue;
- the run driver: the dispatcher answers "when," the driver answers "what happens inside." The driver also holds the run open: a turn is not considered finished until its nested sub-runs are counted in.

State is held by the chat runtime — the inbox, background tasks, the progress tree, cancellation; every chat is self-contained, and tools find their chat through an ambient scope, not a global variable. The chat registry opens and closes them, and the agent runtime gives the instance a shared set of capabilities: tools, plugins, the event bus.

# Moment
Before the first turn and at the top of every next one. The only point where a running turn can receive something that was not there when it started.

# What breaks
Without the inbox, a reply into a busy chat is either lost or starts a second parallel turn. And a background call has nowhere to return its result — so a long tool must hold the turn again.

description.v: The start of every turn: what actually ships to the provider is assembled from the contributors' notes — prompt segments, history, and the set of tools visible to the model right now.

doc.v:
# Input and output
Input: chat history, working memory, attached skills, the feature catalog, project state. Output: one request to the provider and the list of tools declared to the model for this turn.

# Description
The prompt does not sit ready in a file — it is rebuilt each time from every contributor's note: a feature brings its own piece of text and its own tools, a plugin adds a description of what it does, an attached skill inserts its own text, working memory mixes in keys prefixed context:.

What happens next:

- the assembler folds the segments and the history into one request and decides what did not fit. Trimming happens here, not at the provider, because the provider does not know which segment matters more;
- the tool-set registry decides which tools the model sees now and which unfold on request: declaring everything at once is expensive and harmful;
- the feature catalog keeps a tool and its owning feature's prompt as one delivery; let them drift apart and the result is confidently wrong behavior.

The prompt stays a list of segments, not a string: every piece carries a source and a role. The same source produces both what ships to the model and the color-coded preview a human sees, so what is shown and what is sent cannot diverge by construction.

# Moment
Before every call to the model, not once per turn. Reassembly is mandatory: the previous call's result may have written a working-memory key, attached a skill, or unfolded a new tool set.

# What breaks
This is where the turn's ceiling is set: what is not in the context does not exist for the model, what is not in the tool set will not be called. Bugs at this stage look less like a failure and more like "the model got dumber" — and get chased in the wrong place.

description.v: The middle of the turn: the assembled request leaves through the one gateway and comes back as a response — text, tool calls, or both.

doc.v:
# Input and output
Input: the assembled request and the declared tool set. Output: the model's response — text, a list of calls, or both.

# Description
The step everything else exists for: one half of the turn prepares the model's input, the other interprets its output and keeps that output from doing more than it is allowed to.

The model is the only participant in this diagram whose behavior is not defined by SPLA's code. Its answer is an untrusted input: until it passes admission, it is data, not a command.

One door leads out, whichever provider the turn is going to — a local LM Studio or the cloud through OpenRouter. A stack of wrappers stands around the call:

- substituting the provider's key and address;
- checking the provider is reachable;
- accounting tokens by what the provider actually reported, not by string length;
- a guard against degeneration: noticing the model went in circles, it cancels the generation and asks again.

One call to the model can consist of several attempts — a canceled generation and a retry are still the same turn.

# Moment
Exactly one call per turn. A five-turn run is five calls, and their sum is the turn's cost.

# What breaks
A call made around the gateway lands in neither the token count nor the degeneration guard — and for a cloud provider, the count is not a convenience, it is a bill.

description.v: Right after the model answers: every named call is identified, checked against its schema, and either granted or denied admission. The only place where text legitimately becomes an action.

doc.v:
# Input and output
Input: the model's response with one or more calls. Output: an admitted call that proceeds to execution, or a refusal.

# Description
The model does not execute tools — it names one and hands over arguments. Everything between that name and real work lives here, and the entry point is the same for every tool: native, plugin-supplied, or proxied from a foreign MCP server.

The queue of stages:

- find the tool by name and check the arguments against its schema — this is where the model's invention first meets reality, and a nonexistent name must produce a clear refusal, not an exception from the depths;
- name the "source → sink" edge between trust zones and compute what the zone policy would decide, without actually forbidding anything yet: the policy is measured on live traffic first, then switched on;
- ask permission from the policy, and if it does not know, from a human. This is the one place a turn stops and waits for a human, and a permission holds for the call, not for the session;
- notice the same call with the same arguments has already happened — the second half of the loop guard.

A refusal is a result too: it comes back to the model as the tool's answer and does not break the turn.

# Moment
Between the model's answer and any work, on every call named in that answer.

# What breaks
The order of the stages is itself the security policy. Reordering them silently changes the threat model; bypassing the host entirely strips the call of admission, progress, and accounting all at once.

description.v: An admitted call does the real work: files, the shell, a plugin, a foreign MCP server, a sub-agent. The only part of the turn that touches the outside world.

doc.v:
# Input and output
Input: an admitted call with checked arguments. Output: a result, a background receipt, or an error.

# Description
Who actually does the work:

- basic tools — files, search, the shell: what makes an agent useful in any project at all;
- plugins — everything domain-specific, each in its own load context, responsible for resolving its own native dependencies too;
- a foreign MCP server — its tools are handed to the model as if native, prefixed with the server's name, but they pass through the same stages: a foreign server is a trash can, not a trusted participant;
- a sub-agent — its own turn with its own progress tree; it accepts a free-form prompt, not just a chosen skill, and the price for that is curatability of an outside head.

A long tool must not hold the turn: the turn gets a receipt right away, and the actual result arrives in the chat's inbox — the same path a human reply takes. So execution can finish later than the turn that started it, and that is the normal case, not a failure.

Every call gets a node in the progress tree, so nested and parallel calls are shown exactly as such.

A tool does not walk outward on its own: a path becomes a real address through the workspace, processes are started by the shell session, and what is allowed at all is answered by the capability gate. A secret is resolved by reference at the point of use and never enters the context.

# Moment
Right after admission, within the same turn. Calls from one model answer can run in parallel.

# What breaks
This is where a mistake costs the most: the operating system is the terminal receiver of most edges. The sandbox today is a stub with no restrictions, and that is stated honestly: first the contract and every call routed through it, real isolation later.

description.v: Closing the turn: results become history, a report goes out about what happened, and the cycle decides — one more turn, or the end of the run.

doc.v:
# Input and output
Input: the calls' results and whatever piled up in the inbox. Output: an updated history and a decision — another turn or the end of the run.

# Description
The orchestrator is the backbone itself: assemble context → ask the model → execute the calls → repeat. Everything else in this diagram plugs into it by answering "which step of the cycle do I serve"; whatever does not answer that question is not part of the architecture model.

The run ends when the model named no calls at all — or when Stop or cancellation kills it, along with the queue. As long as calls are being named, turns keep going, and each one starts with a fresh context assembly. Results are appended to history and ship to the model on the next assembly — together with whatever landed in the inbox meanwhile: receipts for finished background calls, sub-agent reports, a human's reply.

The turn reports outward along the way:

- the progress tree shows who started whom and what is running on top of what;
- the event bus broadcasts what happened to every connected client at once — otherwise a second window open on the same chat shows the past;
- the edge ledger remembers what went where: material the zone policy will use to derive default thresholds instead of guessed ones;
- bulk data between tools travels by reference to a blob, bypassing the context: the model does not need to see the content to hand it on.

# Moment
After execution, on every turn.

# What breaks
If the decision to continue is made anywhere but here — inside a tool, or a client — "the end of the run" stops being one point, and "stop" starts meaning different things in different places.

description.v: Not a stage, but what is read and written at any point in the cycle and outlives the turn: history, working memory, blobs, secrets, the token counter.

doc.v:
# Input and output
No input or output of its own: not a step, but a store any step can reach into.

# Description
The only group on this diagram outside the axis of time. Who touches it, and when:

- context assembly reads chat history and working memory;
- the call to the model tops up the token counter;
- execution writes blobs and resolves secret references;
- closing the turn appends to history.

A project here is a provider of storage areas, not a storage itself: the .spla manifest sits next to the code and goes under git; the .spla/ working directory does not — it holds what has no business in the repository. Entering a project is a lease, not ownership: the manifest has one writer, an instance registers itself and lets go on its own.

Working memory has two tiers: the session tier is bound to the chat through an ambient scope, not to the process, so two chats in one process do not confuse their keys; the project tier survives chats. Naming follows namespace:name, and part of the contract is that only context: ships into the prompt automatically.

A blob outlives the call, but not the project: it is the foundation of the data channel that lets tools hand each other bulk content around the model. Secrets sit under the system's own encryption with access lists. The token counter survives a restart: spend on one turn says little, the sum over the project's lifetime is the interesting number.

# Moment
No moment of its own — reached from any turn.

# What breaks
This is exactly why the next turn does not start from zero. Anything that moved into the run's own memory instead disappears with the run — the conversation, and the accumulated knowledge of the project, both.

description.v: The domain: concepts and contracts that know nothing about the protocol, the provider, or the operating system.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Everything that can be explained without naming a single technology: what a turn is, a chat, a zone, a secret, a workspace.

# Description
Home to interfaces (the gateway to the model, the shell, the workspace, the sandbox, chat storage, secret storage) and the concepts around them: an LLM turn's context, the reasoning lever, a trust zone, the progress tree.

Live example: the domain declares that a shell is a session with three actions. How exactly a process gets started on Windows the domain does not know and should not — that is the implementation's business.

# Boundary
Nothing that drags along a specific protocol, a specific provider, or a specific operating system belongs here. The test is simple: if understanding a class requires knowing it is HTTP, or that it is Windows, the class is not from here.

description.v: The tool pipeline: the path a call takes from the name the model spoke to execution — and the context assembly that told the model that name.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Everything around a tool: how the model learns about it, and how its call reaches actual work.

# Description
Two halves of one mechanism:

- context assembly — the composer, the contributor contract, prompt pieces, the feature catalog, tool sets: this is where the model learns what can even be called;
- the call pipeline — the tool host and its stages: parsing the name and arguments, zones, permissions, progress, background.

Also here: the edge ledger, which remembers what went where, and the data channel, which passes bulk content between tools around the prompt.

# Boundary
No specific tools live here — only the path any of them takes. Tools live in the base assembly and in plugins.

description.v: The chat and agent runtime: the conversation's live state and the turn cycle itself.

doc.v:
# What it groups
What lives while work is happening: chats, their state, the spinning cycle, and the guards around it.

# Description
The chat registry and the chat runtime hold state; the agent runtime is the instance's shared set of capabilities; the orchestrator spins the turns. Alongside it, wired straight into the turn: mixing working memory into the prompt, the degeneration guard, the repeated-call tracker, token accounting, launching sub-agents, the event bus.

# Boundary
No contracts here — those live in the domain — and no protocol. This is the layer where contracts become a working machine for one instance.

description.v: LLM providers: integrations with whoever actually answers the request.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Code that knows the specifics of particular providers, and only that.

# Description
The shared half is the OpenAI-compatible protocol client: build the request, read the stream, pull out tool calls. The provider-specific halves are LM Studio (local models on the owner's machine) and OpenRouter (the cloud through one key), each with its own native API for the management knobs.

# Boundary
Nothing but talking to the provider. Token accounting, the degeneration guard, and key substitution live in the wrappers around the gateway — otherwise every new integration would regrow them from scratch.

description.v: The service and the protocol: the agent behind a wire, clients connecting from outside.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Everything that makes the agent reachable not from inside the process, but over a protocol.

# Description
The service host holds the runtime, the router parses client messages, the turn dispatcher and the run driver turn incoming traffic into work. From here, outward: SPLA as an MCP server for foreign agents, connections to foreign MCP servers, the registry of running instances, resolving a user's domain identity.

# Boundary
No turn logic here — only delivery. The pivot to a service means the embedded mode is also a client that raised a service inside itself, not a separate branch of code.

description.v: Plugins and tools: what the agent can actually do with its hands.

doc.v:
# What it groups
The tools themselves, and the mechanism that plugs them in.

# Description
The base assembly gives the minimum any project needs: files, search, the shell. Everything domain-specific arrives as plugins: the manager finds and queries them, a separate load context keeps each one's assemblies apart — native dependencies included.

# Boundary
The line runs along "does any project need this." A "no" means a plugin, even when the implementation is trivial.

description.v: Clients: the windows through which people talk to the agent.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Applications with no turn logic of their own — they display, and they send.

# Description
The Vue web client is the main face: chat, the workspace, the editor. The command line is one-off runs and starting the service. The desktop shell is a window, a project hub, and an embedded browser with the same web client inside.

# Boundary
One chat render for everyone. Any feature added around the protocol reaches exactly one client and is invisible to the rest.

description.v: External: participants we do not write and do not control.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Two: the model, whose answer is an untrusted input, and the operating system, where an action becomes real and irreversible.

# Description
Both are separated into their own group for the same reason: neither one's behavior is defined by SPLA's code, and both are talked to through contracts, not straight from a tool.

# Boundary
Our responsibility ends here. The conversation with both sides goes through contracts — the gateway to the model, the sandbox with its workspace and shell — never straight out of a tool.

description.v: The model island: the source of untrusted input.

doc.v:
# What it groups
One participant — the model itself, because trust in its answer differs from trust in everything else.

# Description

doc.v:
# What it groups

description.v: The service process: where the agent lives and a turn happens.

doc.v:

description.v: The plugin load context: its own set of assemblies inside the service process.

doc.v:

description.v: The child process: what the agent started through the shell.

doc.v:
# What it groups
The shell, the sandbox, and the operating system on the other side of a launch.

# Description

description.v: A foreign process or network: whatever executes somewhere else.

doc.v:
# What it groups

# Description

description.v: The domain: concepts and contracts that know nothing about the protocol, the provider, or the operating system.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Everything that can be explained without naming a single technology: what a turn is, a chat, a zone, a secret, a workspace.

# Description

description.v: The tool pipeline: the path a call takes from the name the model spoke to execution — and the context assembly that told the model that name.

doc.v:
# What it groups
Everything around a tool: how the model learns about it, and how its call reaches actual work.

# Description
Two halves of one mechanism:

- context assembly — the composer, the contributor contract, prompt pieces, the feature catalog, tool sets: this is where the model learns what can even be called;

description.v: The chat and agent runtime: the conversation's live state and the turn cycle itself.

doc.v:

# Boundary

description.v: LLM providers: integrations with whoever actually answers the request.

doc.v:
# What it groups

# Description

doc.v:

description.v: Plugins and tools: what the agent can actually do with its hands.

doc.v:

description.v: Clients: the windows through which people talk to the agent.

doc.v:

description.v: A context contributor: a participant that lays its own piece of text and its own tools into the system prompt before the call to the model.
The one door out to the model. One method: go to the model with this request and return the answer.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides the ways of talking to specific LLM providers.

# Description
Wherever a turn is headed — a local LM Studio on the owner's machine or the cloud through OpenRouter — it goes through one door. Behind the door stands a stack of wrappers, and only behind that, the chosen provider.

Why one door: everything that needs doing around every call to the model gets hung here once and reaches every provider at once:

- count the tokens actually spent and record them against the project's bill;
- notice the model went in circles and ask it to regenerate;
- substitute the provider's key or address;
- remember how the call turned out.

# Moment
The middle of the turn. Exactly one call to the gateway per turn; a five-turn run is five passes through the gateway, and their sum is the cost of the run.

# If bypassed
Every new integration would regrow token accounting, the degeneration guard, and key substitution from scratch — and drift from the others in the small details that surface a month later.

description.v: A wrapper around the call to the model: receives the request, may change it, passes it on, and inspects whatever comes back.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides everything done around a call to the model, so that neither the provider nor the turn cycle knows about it.

# Description
The call to the model does not go straight through — it passes a stack of wrappers, like a row of inspectors, each with its own job. A wrapper receives the request, does its part, calls the next one, and gets back an answer it is entitled to inspect and even cancel.

Who stands in the stack today:

- substituting the provider's credentials — key and address — before sending;
- checking the provider is reachable and in working order at all;
- accounting tokens by what the provider actually reported, not by string length;
- a guard against degeneration: if the model went in circles, the generation is canceled and asked for again;
- recording the outcome: how this call turned out.

Every wrapper declares a stage — its place in the stack. A stage is not decoration: the degeneration guard only makes sense where the stream of generation is visible, and nowhere earlier.

Deliberately built symmetric to the tool-call pipeline: two different calls outward — to the model and to a tool — are wrapped the same way, and that saves a whole class of explanations.

# Moment
Around every call to the model, so once per turn. One call can consist of several attempts — a canceled generation and a retry are still the same turn.

# If bypassed
Logic grown onto the provider instead of a wrapper reaches only that provider. From there it either gets copy-pasted into the next one, or quietly lost on it.

description.v: One stage on a tool call's path: receives the call, does its own job, and passes it on — or does not.
The capability gate: four questions about what the turn is even allowed to do — read a path, write a path, launch processes, reach the network.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides the answer to "is this even allowed" — so a tool needs to know neither the policy nor the operating system.

# Description
The gate is not permission for a specific call, it is a coarse frame: can this path be read at all, written at all, can anything be launched, can the network be reached.

What that looks like in practice:

- the file-read tool asks "can this path be read" and on "no" returns a refusal, not someone else's file;
- the shell tool asks "can processes be launched at all" and on "no" does not start — instead of failing halfway;
- a tool reaching the network asks about the network separately: files and network are different capabilities.

Today there is one implementation and it allows everything. That is a deliberate first step: first every call must be routed through the gate, then real restrictions appear inside it. Until the gate sits on the call's path, there is nowhere to attach a restriction at all.

# Moment
Execution, from inside a tool — already after the call has been admitted.

# Trap
The gate is bypassed exactly one way — through the shell, and that is stated plainly. A tool allowed to launch processes gets everything else for free: a shell command reads and writes whatever it likes. That is why real isolation belongs on execution, in the sandbox, not as a longer list of questions here.

description.v: The shell as a session: a command may not finish, it may ask — and the turn answers with a separate call, into that same live session.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides launching operating-system processes and, above all, waiting on a live command — one that asked a question and is waiting for an answer.

# Description
The ordinary "run a command and return the output" breaks on the first command that asks something: the system requests confirmation, an installer asks "continue? [y/N]" — and a one-shot run just hangs until it times out, reporting nothing.

So the shell here is a session of three actions:

- run a command; control returns once it exited, once it asked something, or once it went quiet past the idle threshold — whichever happens first;
- resume the session: hand it a line of input, or simply wait longer;
- kill the session together with its whole process tree, taking whatever it had printed.

Live example: the model starts an installation, it prints a question and goes quiet. The turn gets not a timeout but the question's text and a session id; the question is visible to the model, and the next call feeds "y" into that same session.

Sessions belong to the chat, not the process: closing the chat means killing its sessions, and the cap on live sessions is counted per chat, not shared out blind between chats that know nothing of each other.

# Moment
Execution — only for an admitted call, and only if the capability gate allows launching processes.

# If bypassed
A process launched around the shell is one nobody kills when the chat closes, and one you cannot ask what it is waiting for.

description.v: The workspace: translates the logical path the model operates on into a real address on the machine — and back.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides the file system: where "src/main.cs" actually sits, and whether there is a file system there at all.

# Description
The model says "read src/main.cs." Where that actually is depends on how the agent is running: locally — the project folder on the owner's disk, on a server — a specific domain user's personal area, embedded — something else again. The translation lives here, and only here.

What it does: translate a path both ways, check a file or folder exists, read and write content, list folders and files.

Live example: the file-read tool knows nothing about disks or servers — it asks for the path to be translated. A path pointing past the workspace boundary is simply not translated, and the tool gets a refusal instead of someone else's file. The reverse translation is needed to show the model a found file by its own path, not by the host's absolute address.

# Moment
Execution — on every call that touches files.

# If bypassed
A tool that reaches the file system directly only works where it was written: on a server it will reach into someone else's area, embedded it will reach into nothing. That is exactly why one build of the core runs locally, on a server, and embedded: what changes is the path translation, not the tools.

description.v: The sandbox: a bundle of the three things a turn touches the outside world with — the workspace, the shell, and the capability gate.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides the entire outside world available to a turn: a tool gets the sandbox and has no other way out.

# Description
The sandbox here is not "isolation" as such, it is one bundle of three: what to read and write with (the workspace), what to launch with (the shell — it may be absent, and then execution is simply off), and what is allowed at all (the gate).

Every chat has its own sandbox in the part that carries live state:

- the workspace boundary is shared — it must read the same for everyone;
- the gate is shared for the same reason;
- the shell is a chat's own, because it is where open sessions live.

While the shell was one for everyone, the phrase "kill this chat's sessions" could not even be said, and the cap on live sessions was split between chats that knew nothing about each other.

Today the implementation is a stub that restricts nothing, and that is recorded honestly. The point of the first step is that a restriction gets inserted in one place later, not into fifty tools.

# Moment
Execution. Everything a turn does with the outside world passes through here — and this is where the host takes on that risk.

# Trap
The word "sandbox" promises more than exists today. There is not one real restriction yet — only the contract, and the obligation for everyone to go through it.

description.v: Chat storage: save, load, list, archive, delete along with everything attached to a chat.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides where conversation history lives: today, files in the project's working directory; tomorrow, a database.

# Description
A chat is a message history, and it must survive a restart: a closed window must not mean a lost conversation. The store holds chats by id and lists them with the freshest first.

What actually happens here:

- a client opened the project's chat list — that is a listing from here;
- a turn appended the model's reply — that is a save here, on closing the turn;
- a human clicked "archive" — the chat vanished from the list but stayed on disk, visible in a separate listing;
- a human deleted a chat — everything attached to it went with it: a summary, backups, attached images.

The "freshest first" order is declared by the contract, not left to the caller: a database will make it its own ORDER BY, a file implementation a sort on read.

# Moment
Outside the cycle. Read during context assembly — history ships to the model — written when the turn closes.

# If bypassed
A record written around the store lands in neither the chat list nor deletion: it stays an orphan nobody shows and nobody cleans up.

description.v: The project provider: lists known projects, shows recent ones, opens by id, creates a new one.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides where the project list comes from and what "open a project" means: a local folder, a server-side user area, something else.

# Description
A project is the root everything else lives around: the workspace, chat history, working memory, secrets, the token counter. The provider answers four questions: what projects are known, which opened recently, open this one, create a new one.

Live example: the project hub in the desktop shell is "list and show recent"; clicking a row is "open by id," and the opening itself records that the project was just opened — so it lands on top next time.

An easy distinction to miss: a project provides storage areas, it does not hold storage. The .spla manifest sits next to the code and goes under git; the .spla/ working directory does not — it holds what has no business in the repository: chat history, memory, counters.

Entering a project is a lease, not ownership: the manifest has one writer, an instance registers itself and lets go on its own. Who holds a project right now is a question for the instance registry, not this one.

# Moment
Before the turn. A project is open before the first chat exists, and it outlives any single turn.

# Trap
A project whose manifest went missing silently drops out of the listing — "known" here means "the manifest is present," not "was opened once."

description.v: Secret storage: put a password or a key, retrieve it by name, list names — never values — grant access.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides how secrets are actually stored: Windows-native encryption and file access rights — for the caller it is simply "put" and "get."

# Description
A secret is a record with fields (login, password, key) living in one of three scopes: personal, project, shared. Scopes never fall through into each other: asked in the project scope, the answer is either from there or "no." Silent substitution of a value from elsewhere never happens.

Live example: a database connection stores not a password but a reference to a secret. At the moment of connecting the reference resolves into a value, goes into the driver, and settles nowhere else — not in chat history, not in the model's context.

Two rules are visible right in the set of actions:

- listing returns keys and field names, never values: a settings list has no use for values;
- an entry carries an access list, and it does meaningful work in the shared scope, where access is granted to domain groups.

# Moment
Execution — the reference resolves at the point of use, not ahead of time "just in case."

# Trap
No tools for working with secrets are given to the model on purpose: it operates on references, and never sees values. The first "convenient" tool to read a secret cancels the whole design at once.

description.v: The instance registry: which copies of SPLA are running right now and which project each is holding. It reports — it does not start or kill anyone.

doc.v:
# What it abstracts
Hides where knowledge of other running copies comes from: lock files next to projects, or querying a remote service.

# Description
Several copies of SPLA can run at once: a window on the desktop, a service on a server, a one-off command-line run. And a project has one writer. The registry answers two questions: what is running now, freshest first, and who holds this particular project.

Live example: a human opens a project already held by another instance. The interface does not stay silent and does not take it away — it shows exactly which window has the project.

Two honesties are built right into the contract:

- an instance registers and deregisters itself; the registry starts and kills nothing — it reports;
- an unreachable instance comes back with the status "could not confirm," not dropped from the list: "it is not there" and "I could not reach it" are different answers, and only one of them is true.

Asking an instance what it is doing is a separate matter: whoever only needs a plain listing does not carry a protocol client along and gets facts from lock files.

# Moment
Before the turn and outside it — on entering a project, and wherever what is currently running is shown.

# Trap
The registry describes intent, not a guarantee: it does not stop a second instance from opening the same project — it only lets you see that one is already busy.

description.v: The chat inbox: a queue of what is addressed to the chat but has no turn of its own to arrive on.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds the incoming queue for one chat and hands it to the turn when the turn looks in.

# Description
What lands in the inbox:

- a reply a human wrote into the chat while a turn is already running;
- a background call's result that came back later than the turn that started it;
- a sub-agent's report on a finished task.

The turn cycle looks into the inbox at the top of every turn, and everything sitting there ships to the model together with the calls' results.

# Moment
Intake — at the top of every turn. Things go in at any moment; they come out strictly there.

# Trap
Without the inbox, a reply into a busy chat is either lost or starts a second parallel turn — and both look, from the human's side, like "the system didn't hear me."

description.v: The turn dispatcher: turns the inbox's contents into a running turn and holds the queue while the turn is going.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Decides when a turn starts. One dispatcher per chat.

# Description
The dispatcher watches the inbox: something's there, it starts a run; nothing is, it waits. While a run is going, the next reply stays in the inbox, so two turns in one chat never happen by construction, not by agreement.

Stop kills everything at once: the current turn and the queue. One button with a predictable meaning — "stop dealing with this chat," not "cancel the last call."

# Moment
Intake: before the first turn and between turns.

# Trap
The dispatcher answers only "when." What happens inside is the run driver's job; conflate them and a stop can kill the turn without killing its sub-runs.

description.v: One run of a turn: connects the dispatcher to the agent cycle and hands out events to subscribers.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Carries one specific turn from start to finish and reports on it outward.

# Description
The driver is separated from the dispatcher on purpose: the dispatcher answers "when," the driver answers "what happens inside." It starts the cycle, hands it the chat's assembled capabilities, and along the way hands out events — a turn started, a piece of an answer arrived, a tool call went out — and clients show them.

The driver also holds the run open: a turn is not considered finished until its nested sub-runs are counted in. A sub-agent launched during execution may finish after its parent, and without this hold the parent turn would close before its own work was done.

# Moment
Intake — for the entire span of one turn, from launch to end.

description.v: One chat's state: the inbox, background tasks, the progress tree, cancellation.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds everything that belongs to one chat and has to die with it.

# Description
Every chat is a self-contained machine: its own inbox, its own background tasks, its own progress tree, its own cancellation, its own shell with open sessions. Two chats in one process do not see each other's state.

Tools find their chat through an ambient scope — that is, by which turn they were called inside of — not through a global variable. That is exactly what makes "kill this chat's sessions" and "stop this chat" phrases that can actually be executed.

# Moment
Outlives the turn: created on opening the chat, closed on closing it.

# Trap
State placed anywhere but the chat runtime (a static field, a process-wide cache) outlives closing the chat and surfaces in the next one — usually as "why does it remember something I never said."

description.v: The registry of the process's open chats: the point where a chat is created and where it is closed.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Knows which chats are currently open in this instance and hands out their runtime by id.

# Description
When a client opens a chat, the registry either finds an already-live runtime or creates a new one; when a chat closes, it takes it down and releases whatever it was holding. A turn always works with a runtime obtained here.

# Moment
Before and after the turn — on opening and closing the chat.

# Trap
This is where an open question sits: plugins get no notification of a chat's lifecycle. A plugin with live state — a COM object, a browser session — does not know when to clean up, and holds the resource until the process ends.

description.v: The agent runtime: the assembled set of capabilities, shared across every chat of the instance.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Assembles once what is expensive to assemble: the tool registry, loaded plugins, the event bus, connected providers.

# Description
An instance has many chats and one set of capabilities: plugins load once, tools register once, events travel on one bus. A chat gets not a copy of all this, but access to the shared set — plus its own state on top.

# Moment
Before the first turn: the runtime is built before the first chat opens.

# Trap
A known limitation: tools register only in the constructor. Adding a tool on the fly — say, when a new MCP server gets connected mid-conversation — is not possible today, and that is an open question, not an oversight.

description.v: The turn cycle: assemble context → ask the model → execute the calls → repeat, until the model stops.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Spins the turn's rounds and decides when the run is over.

# Description
This is the backbone everything else plugs into. One round:

- reassemble the context, including whatever landed in the inbox since last time;
- go to the model exactly once;
- pass the named calls through admission and execute the ones that pass;
- append the results to history and decide whether another round is needed.

The run ends when the model named no calls at all — or when Stop kills it.

# Moment
The whole run: the cycle starts at intake and ends when the last round closes.

# Trap
The check "is this my step of the cycle" is a way to tell whether a new piece even belongs in the architecture model. Whatever does not answer that question is not wired to the backbone.

description.v: Assembles the system prompt and the tool set from the contributors' contributions.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Goes around every context contributor and folds their notes into one prompt with one tool set.

# Description
The composer knows no provider by name — it knows the contributor contract and asks everyone subscribed to it: the working mode, agent features, plugins, skills, working memory, tool sets, the project.

Every contribution is remembered together with its author, so the question "who put this paragraph in the prompt" has an answer, not a guess. A contributor that falls over does not vanish silently: the error is caught and recorded, or a piece of the prompt would disappear without a trace.

# Moment
Context assembly, before every call to the model.

# Trap
The temptation to "just add a couple of lines straight into the prompt" breaks both the preview and accounting at once: what is shown to a human diverges from what is sent to the model.

description.v: A piece of the prompt as an object: source, role, text.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds one prompt fragment together with the answer to where it came from.

# Description
The prompt is a list of such pieces, not one string. Each one carries its author on record (a feature, a plugin, a skill, memory) and a role, so the same list yields two things at once: the flat text that ships to the provider, and the color-coded preview a human sees.

# Moment
Context assembly: pieces are born fresh on every turn.

# Trap
The divergence between what is shown and what is sent is impossible here by construction — but only for as long as nobody glues the prompt together around this list.

description.v: Folds segments and history into what actually ships to the provider.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Turns the list of pieces and the chat history into one request — and decides what did not fit.

# Description
The context window has a limit, and someone has to choose what to sacrifice: old messages, a bulky tool result, an optional prompt segment. The choice is made here, because only here is everything visible at once.

# Moment
Context assembly, at the very end — after every contributor has had its say.

# Trap
Trimming on the provider's side would look cheaper, but the provider does not know which segment matters more: to it, this is all the same text.

description.v: Mixes working-memory keys prefixed context: into the context.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Pulls from working memory the entries that must always be in the prompt, and puts them there without the model asking.

# Description
Keys follow the namespace:name pattern, and the prefix is part of the contract, not decoration:

- context: ships into the prompt on its own, on every turn. This is where what the model must always remember goes: project conventions, the current goal;
- task:, project:, note: the model reads deliberately, with its own tool, when it decides to.

# Moment
Context assembly, on every turn — so a context: key written on the previous step is visible to the model already on the next one.

# Trap
Everything that lands in context: is paid for in tokens on every call to the model. What looks cheap — "let it just sit there" — is a bill growing linearly with the number of turns.

description.v: The agent feature catalog: each feature brings its own piece of prompt and its own tools.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds the list of features and what each one adds: instructional text and a list of tools.

# Description
A feature is the bundle "tools plus the explanation of how to use them." File work brings read and edit tools and the text on how to use them; shell work brings its own of both.

Hence the project rule: change a tool, edit its feature's prompt.md. The prompt and the tool ship as one delivery.

# Moment
Context assembly: the catalog is queried as one of the contributors.

# Trap
Once they drift apart, the instruction and the tool don't produce a refusal — they produce confidently wrong behavior: the model does exactly what is written, and that is already untrue.

description.v: Skills attached to the turn, and their resources.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds the skills switched on for the current conversation and feeds their text and files into the context.

# Description
A skill is external text pulled by an address of the form "source:id." While it is attached, its content takes part in the prompt, and the resources attached to it are available to the model on request.

Trust in a skill is decided by where it came from, not by what it says: text from a personal store and text from someone else's branch are different things, even when the words match.

# Moment
Context assembly — an attached skill is visible to the model starting the next turn.

# Trap
A skill is instructions arriving from outside the conversation. Treating it like an order from the human is wrong for exactly that reason: putting text there is not necessarily a human's doing.

description.v: Tool sets and the levels at which they unfold to the model.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Decides which tools the model sees on this turn, and which exist but are not declared yet.

# Description
There are many tools in the system: base, plugin-supplied, proxied from foreign MCP servers. Declaring them all at once means paying tokens for descriptions this conversation will never need, and burying what actually matters in the list.

So the set unfolds in tiers: part is declared right away, the rest the model requests once it realizes it needs it.

# Moment
Context assembly — the set's composition is decided fresh on every turn.

# Trap
A tool absent from the set does not exist for the model: it will neither call it nor report that it was missing.

description.v: The service: the agent behind a protocol, clients are just windows.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds the agent runtime and talks to clients over a protocol.

# Description
The agent does not live inside a window — it lives behind a protocol. Everything else follows from that:

- a desktop window, the command line, and a browser are different clients of the same agent;
- embedded mode is a client that raised a service inside itself, not a separate branch of code;
- a second window opened on the same chat sees the same thing, because it is connected to the same service.

# Moment
Before and around the turn: the service outlives any single chat.

# Trap
The pivot to a service means "do it quickly right in the client" is a feature the other clients will never have. There is one core: local, on a server, embedded.

description.v: Parses protocol messages and hands them out to their handlers.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Takes a client's message, understands what it is, and passes it to whoever executes it.

# Description
This is where the boundary between client and core runs. A chat reply lands in the inbox from here, a request for the chat list goes to storage, an answer to a permission question goes to admission.

Whatever one client can do, it does through the protocol — and therefore any other client can do it too.

# Moment
Intake: this is where the path of any outside message begins.

# Trap
A feature added around the protocol reaches exactly one client and is invisible to the rest — including its own author, logged in from another machine.

description.v: The main client: chat, workspace, editor.

doc.v:
# What it is to us
The system's main face: what people talk to the agent through.

# Description
The web client shows the chat, the running turn's progress tree, the project's files, and the editor. It talks to the core only over the protocol — it has no direct road inward.

The chat's render is one across the system: the desktop shell shows this same client inside an embedded browser, not its own copy of the interface.

# Boundary
The client is a window, not a brain. No turn logic lives in it and none should: it shows what the service sent and sends what the human did.

description.v: The command line: one-off runs and starting the service.

doc.v:
# What it is to us
A second client of the same agent, and, at the same time, a way to raise the service.

# Description
The command line is for where a window is superfluous:

- a one-off run — set a task, get a result, exit; this is how batch jobs like meeting summaries get done;
- starting a service other clients then connect to.

# Boundary
The same agent, the same protocol. A one-off run differs from a chat not in how it's built, but in that after the last turn nobody is waiting for a next reply.

description.v: The desktop shell: a window, a project hub, an embedded web client.

doc.v:
# What it is to us
The application on the desktop: what a shortcut launches.

# Description
The shell gives three things: an operating-system window, a project hub (choose what to work on), and an embedded browser hosting the same web client. It has no chat interface of its own on purpose — otherwise two diverging renders would need maintaining.

# Boundary
A platform trap that cost time to debug: a ContentControl's content stays in the tree while IsVisible=False, so switching views is done by replacing Border.Child from code, not by visibility.

description.v: A user's domain identity via NTLM/Negotiate.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Answers "who just connected" using Windows domain facilities.

# Description
On a server the agent is one, and there are many people. Identity is resolved once, on connection, and everything else follows: every user has their own file area, and shared access is granted through domain groups.

# Moment
Before the turn — on establishing the connection, not on every call.

# Trap
Identity re-checked on every call would cost a domain round trip right where work is happening; identity checked once forever would outlive a user switch. Here the connection is chosen as the boundary.

description.v: LLM. The root of the chain: the request leaves from it, and everything that happened during the turn returns to it.

doc.v:
# What it is to us
The one participant whose behavior is not defined by SPLA's code. Everything else in this diagram exists to prepare its input, interpret its output, and keep that output from doing more than it is allowed to.

# Description
The model does not execute anything itself. It receives the assembled prompt with history and the list of available tools, and returns text, tool calls, or both. The work behind those calls is done by the system — and only after admission.

The model lives either on the owner's machine (LM Studio) or in the cloud (OpenRouter); for the turn the difference is only who pays and how fast the answer arrives.

# Boundary
Its answer is an untrusted input: it is data, not a command, until it passes admission. Text that arrives from the model and looks like an order does not become one for that reason.

description.v: The order of the middleware wrapped around one call to the model.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Declares which wrappers stand around a call to the model, and in what order.

# Description
The order is recorded in one place, by stage, not assembled from whoever registered first. A stage says where the wrapper belongs: substituting keys — before sending, token accounting — where the answer is already counted, the degeneration guard — where the stream of generation is visible.

# Moment
Built once, applied on every call to the model.

# Trap
A stage is not decoration. A degeneration guard placed in the wrong spot simply will not see what it was written to see.

description.v: The Output stage: notices generation has degenerated and asks for another attempt.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Watches the stream the model is printing and catches the moment it goes in circles.

# Description
A model sometimes falls into repetition: the same phrase, the same piece of code, an endless list. The wrapper sees it in the stream of generation, cancels the attempt, and asks it to regenerate — the call's context is kept, only the failed attempt is discarded.

Two guards work against a loop, and each is blind alone:

- this one sees the stream of generation but not which tools are being called;
- the repeat tracker at admission sees tool calls but not the text.

# Moment
Around the call to the model, at the stage where output happens.

# Trap
A live repro of the read_file ↔ run_shell loop from August 24, 2026 was only partly untangled: the combination "text plus calls" is not fully covered by either guard alone.

description.v: Catches repeated tool calls with the same arguments.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Remembers the run's recent calls and notices when the same tool gets called with the same arguments again.

# Description
Looping rarely looks like repeated text; more often it is a model reading the same file, running the same command, and reading the same file again. The tracker compares calls and raises the alarm once the loop has closed.

# Moment
Admission — before execution, on every call.

# Trap
Timestamps in tool results break the comparison: results identical in meaning become different by hash, and the loop hides. This is an established cause of misses, not a guess.

description.v: Counts the real tokens the provider reported and adds them to the project's counter.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Takes the actual spend out of the provider's response and appends it to the project's bill.

# Description
What gets counted is what the provider said, not an estimate by string length. The estimate diverges from fact enough that decisions cannot be based on it — and decisions are based on the bill: which model to call, what to put into context:, how much history to drag along.

# Moment
Around every call to the model, so once per turn.

# Trap
The provider sometimes returns zeros where spend actually happened: an observed behavior, not a hypothesis. The counter shows what it was told — it is not obligated to silently under-report.

description.v: Everything known about one call to the model while it is in progress.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds one call's state: the request, the chosen provider, the reasoning lever, whatever has arrived in the answer so far.

# Description
A call and an attempt are different things. The degeneration guard can cancel a generation and ask again; the call's context survives such attempts, the attempt itself does not. Wrappers read and extend this context, passing it along the stack.

# Moment
Lives exactly as long as one call to the model — that is, within the turn.

description.v: Which providers are connected, and who serves the current chat.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds the list of connected providers and answers who serves this particular chat.

# Description
A provider is split in two, and it is not a minor implementation detail:

- the conversation goes over the OpenAI-compatible protocol — the shared half for everyone;
- managing models (what's loaded, what settings exist) goes over the specific provider's own API.

Attempts to merge them into one client kept breaking, again and again, on differences in the management knobs.

# Moment
Before the turn — when choosing who to talk to; and on every call — to know who to go to.

# Trap
A rule of work that is not up for debate: the model in the owner's LM Studio is never loaded, unloaded, or swapped. Whatever is already loaded is what gets used.

description.v: The half shared by every provider: chat over the OpenAI-compatible protocol.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Talks to any provider that understands the OpenAI protocol: builds the request, reads the response stream, pulls tool calls out of it.

# Description
Compatibility saves a whole class of work: a new provider speaking this protocol connects almost for free. But compatibility is always partial, and the differences only show up on a live rig.

Measured facts, not documentation:

- LM Studio accepts an image as image_url and refuses video_url — video does not travel over the wire, but frames sent as a batch work;
- token spend during streamed output does not always arrive as promised.

# Moment
The call to the model — inside the gateway, behind the stack of wrappers.

# Trap
The provider's documentation disagreed with the measured fact three times in a row. Behavior gets checked by measurement, not by reading.

description.v: LM Studio: local models on the owner's machine.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Connects to models running locally in LM Studio: conversation over the compatible protocol, model info over the native API.

# Description
A local model costs nothing in money and never leaves the machine, which is why most of the work happens here. In exchange, there are limits: whatever is loaded is what there is to talk to.

# Moment
The call to the model, when the chat is served by this provider.

# Trap
A firm rule: the model in the owner's LM Studio is never loaded, unloaded, or swapped by the agent. It uses only what a human already loaded.

description.v: OpenRouter: cloud models through one key.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Gives access to cloud models from various vendors through one key and one address.

# Description
When a local model is not enough, the turn goes to the cloud. One key instead of a dozen accounts is the only reason it is wired up this way.

# Moment
The call to the model, when the chat is served by this provider.

# Trap
The only participant in this diagram whose calls are paid for in money. Token accounting here is not a convenience for observation — it is a bill.

description.v: The reasoning lever: how much the model should think about this turn.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Translates the intent "think longer" into what a specific provider actually understands.

# Description
There is no common standard: providers offer three different axes — an effort level, a token budget, an on/off thinking mode. The lever reduces them to one choice on SPLA's side and lays it back out on the wire.

# Moment
Assembling the call to the model — decided before sending, on every turn.

# Trap
"The provider didn't say" does not mean "not allowed." But nothing goes out on the wire that was not declared explicitly either: guessing a parameter absent from the spec is a way to get refused for no reason.

description.v: The tool registry and the entry point for every call.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds every tool there is and accepts every call, wherever it comes from.

# Description
Three kinds of tools live under one roof: base, plugin-supplied, and proxied from foreign MCP servers. For the model there is no difference — it sees one list; for a call there is no difference either — it travels one path, through the stage pipeline.

# Moment
Admission — this is where every call's path begins.

# Trap
Bypassing the host strips a call of three things at once: permissions, progress, and accounting. And quietly: the call will still work, nobody will just know about it.

description.v: The order of stages every tool call passes through.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Declares the composition and order of the stages on a call's path.

# Description
The stages are arranged not by taste but by meaning: first understand what tool and what arguments, then which zones the call moves between, then ask permission, and only then execute. Progress and background get hung on where the call is already admitted.

# Moment
Built once, applied to every call.

# Trap
The order of stages is itself the security policy. Reordering it changes the threat model silently: tests keep passing while permission ends up being asked after the deed is already done.

description.v: Finds the tool by name and checks its arguments against the schema.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Matches what the model named against what actually exists.

# Description
The first stage where the model's invention meets reality. A tool by that name may not exist at all; arguments may not fit the schema; a required field may be missing.

The answer to all of it is a clear refusal that comes back to the model as the call's result: "no such tool," "field path is required." The model then corrects itself on the next turn.

# Moment
Admission — the very first stage, before any checks or permissions.

# Trap
An exception from the depths instead of a refusal is the worst outcome: the run crashes exactly where it should have just gotten a "no."

description.v: Asks for permission on a call — from the policy or from a human.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Decides whether this specific call may go ahead, and stops the turn to ask a human when needed.

# Description
The policy is asked first: a rule may allow reading inside the project and forbid writing outside it. If the policy does not know, the question goes to a human — and the turn waits for the answer.

This is the one place a turn stops and waits for a live decision.

# Moment
Admission — after the call is resolved and before execution.

# Trap
A permission holds for the call, not for the session: a "yes" to one call does not become a "yes" to everything similar for the rest of the conversation.

description.v: Holds and applies admission decisions, including grants on an edge.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Remembers decisions already made and applies them to new calls.

# Description
A decision can be one-off ("yes, to this exact call") or standing ("this tool, in this project — always"). Standing ones are tied to an edge: not "to whom," but "from where to where" — source to sink.

The split with zones works like this: a zone answers who is allowed to talk to whom, a permission answers what exactly is allowed within that conversation. Accounting for resource addresses happens here.

# Moment
Admission — on every call; and in the settings interface, when a human revisits what has been granted.

# Trap
A standing permission outlives the conversation. What was granted once as "always" is something a human forgets sooner than the system does.

description.v: Zone shadow check: computes what the zone policy would decide, without forbidding anything.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Runs the zone policy against live calls and records its verdicts without applying them.

# Description
Shadow before enforcement is deliberate: first the real traffic shows how many calls the policy would have cut and which ones exactly, then the decision to switch it on is made. Otherwise the first false refusal wrecks trust in the whole zone model — and it gets turned off entirely instead of one rule getting fixed.

# Moment
Admission — before permission is asked.

# Trap
The shadow is easy to leave switched on forever: it breaks nothing, and so it never reminds anyone it's still there.

description.v: Zone (island): an area within which trust is uniform.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Describes a stretch of the system where everything is treated as equally trusted.

# Description
A zone's root is the directory carrying the .spla manifest. Inside one zone, calls are uninteresting — everything there is ours. What's interesting is a crossing between zones: from the project's own code into a foreign MCP server, from a plugin into the operating system.

So the unit of accounting is not the node but the edge "source → sink": the danger is not a participant on its own, but the transition.

# Moment
Admission — zones take part in classifying every call.

# Trap
A zone is not a list of folders. Until a transition is named as an edge, there is nothing to hang a refusal on.

description.v: Determines which islands this call moves between.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Looks at a call and says which zone it comes from and which it lands in.

# Description
Live example: a file-read tool called inside the project reads a file of that same project — an edge inside the zone, boring. The same tool reading a file from an outside folder is an edge going out, already worth questions. A call to a foreign MCP server is an edge into a zone with no trust at all.

# Moment
Admission — before the policy or a human says yes or no.

# Trap
Classifying the edge is exactly what tells a zone apart from a list of folders. A mistake here quietly turns a dangerous crossing into a boring one.

description.v: A ledger of crossed edges: what went where over the run's lifetime.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Records every crossed edge: from where, to where, with what.

# Description
The ledger exists so the zone policy's thresholds don't have to be invented. From what accumulates it is visible which transitions happen constantly (so forbidding them would break normal work) and which are one-offs (so they are worth showing a human).

# Moment
Closing the turn — the ledger fills in from calls actually executed.

# Trap
Without the ledger, policy thresholds would come out of thin air — and switching on restrictions for the first time would hit ordinary work.

description.v: Sends a call to the background and returns the turn a receipt.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Relieves the turn of the obligation to wait on a long tool.

# Description
Building a project takes a minute; walking a large file tree takes longer. Holding the turn all that time means holding the human too: they cannot ask or correct anything.

So the call goes to the background, and the turn gets a receipt — "started, id such-and-such" — and continues its round. The finished result arrives in the chat's inbox the same way a human reply does, and gets picked up at the top of the nearest turn.

# Moment
Execution — right after admission, for tools flagged as long-running.

# Trap
An answer from the model after the receipt is an answer to "started," not to "done." A turn that treats the receipt as the result draws conclusions from nothing.

description.v: Gives a call a node in the progress tree.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Makes a running call visible: creates it a node and updates its state while it works.

# Description
Every call gets its own place in the tree: under the turn, or, if another call started it, under that one. So the interface shows not "work in progress" but "searching files inside a sub-agent's task."

# Moment
Execution — the node appears before work begins and closes after it ends.

# Trap
Progress is a tree, not a status line: nested and parallel calls must be shown as nested and parallel, or a long run looks stuck.

description.v: Basic tools: files, search, shell.

doc.v:
# What it is to us
The assembly with the minimum an agent needs to be useful in any project at all.

# Description
Reading and writing files, searching content, listing directories, running commands — this is what an agent spends most of its time on in any task. That is why these tools live in the core and are always present, without plugins or setup.

# Boundary
Anything domain-specific — a database, a browser, documents — must live in a plugin. The line runs along "does any project need this"; "no" means a plugin.

description.v: Finds, loads, and queries plugins.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Discovers installed plugins, brings them up, and asks each what it can do.

# Description
A plugin brings its own tools, a piece of prompt, and — if it has settings — its own settings editor. The interface shows this editor without knowing what is inside: to it, a plugin's settings are an opaque blob.

# Moment
Before the turn: plugins are brought up when the agent runtime is built.

# Trap
The interface has no right to know a single plugin by name. The first "if this is the SQL plugin, show this tab" turns a set of plugins into a list hardcoded into the core.

description.v: A separate load context for each plugin's assemblies.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Keeps one plugin's assemblies apart from the core and from other plugins.

# Description
Two plugins easily bring different versions of the same library. Without separation, whoever loaded first wins, and the second one fails somewhere unexpected. A plugin's own load context settles this by construction.

# Moment
Before the turn — when the plugin loads.

# Trap
The context must resolve native libraries too, not just managed assemblies. Without that, dependencies like SNI are not found, and the plugin fails somewhere other than where it broke — and the investigation goes off in the wrong direction.

description.v: A foreign MCP server's tool, handed to the model as its own.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Represents a foreign tool so the model can call it alongside native ones.

# Description
An external MCP server brings its own list of tools. Each one shows up for the model prefixed with the server's name — so names don't clash and it's clear whose tool it is — and is called the same way any other is: through the same stage pipeline.

# Moment
Execution — the call goes outward, to the foreign server.

# Trap
A foreign server is a trash can, not a trusted participant. Its tool descriptions were not written by us, and its answer is just as untrusted an input as the model's.

description.v: A connection to an external MCP server.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds a live connection to one external server: the handshake, the tool list, calls.

# Description
The transport is chosen by the server's own specification — a process running alongside with standard input/output, or an HTTP address — and it makes no difference to the rest of the diagram: nothing upstream can tell.

# Moment
Before the turn — on connecting; and on every call to a proxied tool.

# Trap
A server can drop mid-conversation, and its tools vanish from the set. To the model this looks like a capability disappearing, and it has to be told in words.

description.v: A spawned sub-agent with its own turn and its own progress tree.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Launches a separate turn inside a tool call and returns its outcome as the result.

# Description
A sub-agent is useful when a task is cheaper to hand to a separate head than to drag through the main conversation: walk twenty files and return a digest, test a hypothesis, gather facts.

It has its own context and its own progress sub-tree — so you can see what it's doing, not just that "a call is in progress." The parent turn does not close until the sub-agent is counted in.

# Moment
Execution — like an ordinary tool call, except a whole cycle spins inside it.

# Trap
A sub-agent accepts a free-form prompt, not just a chosen skill. The price paid for that is curatability: what exactly was sent to the outside head is set at the call site, not by pre-vetted text.

description.v: The turn's progress tree: who started whom, and what stands on what.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds the structure of work in progress: call nodes, their nesting, their state.

# Description
A flat status line shows the latest event and lies about everything else. The tree shows the truth: three calls running in parallel, a sub-agent working inside one of them, a file search open inside that.

Clients draw this tree live — it is the answer to "what is the system doing right now."

# Moment
Lives the whole turn: nodes are created on execution, and the tree belongs entirely to the chat.

# Trap
It replaced the flat progress channel exactly because that one could show neither nesting nor parallelism — and those are exactly what's needed.

description.v: A route for bulk data between tools, around the model's context.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Passes one tool's result to another without routing it through the prompt.

# Description
One tool exports a hundred-thousand-row table, a second one has to process it. That will not fit through the context — and should not: the model does not need to see the content to hand it on.

So the result is placed into blob storage, and only a description enters the context: what it is, how much of it there is, under which reference it sits. The model operates on the reference.

# Moment
Execution — on one call's way out, and the next call's way in.

# Trap
A reference with no meaningful description is useless: the model will not pass on something it doesn't understand.

description.v: The runtime's event bus: everything connected clients know at once.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Broadcasts what happened to every connected client at once.

# Description
An event is not an answer to a request but an announcement: a turn started, a piece of the model's answer arrived, progress changed, the theme switched. Whoever is connected, receives it.

# Moment
Closing the turn, and throughout its work — events go out as things happen, not at the end.

# Trap
Answering one client instead of broadcasting to all is exactly how a second window open on the same chat ends up showing the past without knowing it.

description.v: The agent's working memory: two tiers, session and project.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds "key — value" records the agent itself puts in and reads back.

# Description
Two tiers with different fates:

- session — bound to the chat by an ambient scope, not to the process; the chat ends, and so does this memory;
- project — outlives chats and restarts; this is accumulated knowledge about the project.

Keys follow namespace:name, and the prefix decides how a record reaches the model: context: ships into the prompt on its own, task:, project:, note: the model reads deliberately.

# Moment
Context assembly reads; execution writes — at the model's own request.

# Trap
Planned but not built: a wildcard key filter and a value condition on listing. Listing today is coarse, and a large memory gets paged through whole.

description.v: Storage for bulk data that tools point to by reference.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Holds large chunks of data and hands out references to them.

# Description
Anything that should not travel through the prompt lands here: a table export, a screenshot, a large file's content. Tools trade references, the model sees a description.

A blob outlives a call, but not the project: this is working storage, not an archive.

# Moment
Execution — written on a call's way out, read on the next call's way in.

description.v: Resolves a secret reference into a value — at the point of use.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Turns a reference to a secret into a real value exactly where it is needed.

# Description
Connection settings hold not a password but a reference. The moment a tool is about to connect, the reference resolves into a value, goes into the driver, and settles nowhere — not in chat history, not in the prompt, not in the log.

# Moment
Execution — at the point of use, not ahead of time "just in case."

# Trap
An open question: the default policy today is permissive. That is, more is allowed by default than would be ideal, and narrowing it is still ahead.

description.v: A counter of tokens spent, for the project's whole lifetime.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Accumulates token spend and survives a restart.

# Description
Sits as a file in the project's working directory, topped up on every call to the model. Spend on a single turn says little; the sum is the interesting number — it shows the price of the habit of leaving too much in the prompt.

# Moment
The call to the model — topped up on every turn.

description.v: SPLA as an MCP server for foreign agents.

doc.v:
# What it's busy with
Exposes SPLA's tools outward, so a foreign agent can use them.

# Description
The other side of connecting foreign servers: here, we are the server. A foreign agent sees our tools and calls them with its own protocol; calls still travel the same path through the stage pipeline, with the same permissions.

Progress and cancellation are wired outward: a foreign agent sees that work is happening and can interrupt it.

# Moment
Outside the turn cycle: a separate entry point into the system, parallel to the clients.

# Trap
Resources are not handed out, and that is not an oversight: the dispute over whether bypassing the pipeline is a property of resources themselves, or a detail of our implementation, is not settled.

description.v: Files, processes, network — everything outside SPLA's trust.

doc.v:
# What it is to us
The terminal receiver of most edges: the place where an action becomes real and irreversible.

# Description
A file read, a process launched, a request sent — this is where whatever the turn started ends. Beyond it starts someone else's responsibility: user rights, domain policy, the antivirus, the network.

# Boundary
This is exactly where the chain leads that costs the most when it goes wrong: inside the system, a call can be canceled and asked again, here it cannot. That is why the sandbox sits on execution, right at the boundary, and not somewhere earlier.
